idiom_name: typed map guarded by sync.RWMutex plus golang.org/x/sync/singleflight
implementation_notes: The standard library ships no cache, so the in-process form is a plain map plus sync.RWMutex (the sync package's guidance is to prefer a plain map with locking over sync.Map for general use), with entries carrying a time.Time deadline and expiry handled lazily on read plus a sweep or janitor. The miss path is collapsed with golang.org/x/sync/singleflight so a hot key's expiry does not fan out into one source-of-truth read per goroutine, and the write path commits to the source of truth and then deletes the key. Go's goroutine-per-request model makes the per-key single-flight group the idiomatic replacement for a lock held across a load.
pitfalls: sync.Map is not a drop-in for a general cache: it pays off for stable, mostly read-only key sets, while a plain map with RWMutex is simpler and faster for mixed read/write workloads.
Storing pointers or slices in the map and mutating them outside the lock is a data race the cache cannot see - store immutable values or clones.
TTL alone only hides entries: without a sweep, expired keys leak, so pair lazy expiry with a bounded size or a janitor goroutine.

variants.name: go-redis + singleflight over a shared Redis
variants.idiom_name: go-redis GET/SET with TTL and DEL after the store write, guarded by singleflight
variants.implementation_notes: When instances must share the cache the store moves to Redis: go-redis performs GET/SET/MGET/DEL with a TTL and an encoded payload, and singleflight still guards the per-process miss path so a cold key is loaded once per instance. The ordering rule is unchanged - write the source of truth, then DEL the key, never the reverse - and a Redis error is treated as a miss so the request degrades to the store. MGET and pipelines are the Go-side answer to chatty per-key reads.
pitfalls: A Redis error must be treated as a miss (or handled explicitly); propagating it turns a cache outage into a request outage.
DEL only after the store commit: deleting first leaves a window in which a reader re-caches the pre-update value.
Keys need a namespace and a version, and Redis only evicts when maxmemory-policy is configured - otherwise the cache grows until it is full.
